title: Hubble peers deeply into the Eagle Nebula
caption: The northwestern part of the Eagle Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 16, NGC 6611 · constellation Serpens Cauda · about 7000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Very bright young stars shine out of glowing gas in this Hubble view of the Eagle Nebula, also called Messier 16. Hubble looked at the region's northwestern side, far from its middle.

The stars and the gas are related. The stars formed from the same cloud of material and now belong to an open cluster, cataloged as NGC 6611. These energetic youngsters give off ultraviolet radiation, which makes the surrounding nebula glow.

The cluster was discovered in the mid-eighteenth century, but the fainter nebula took almost two more decades to be noticed, when Charles Messier recorded it. The most famous part of the Eagle Nebula, its tall columns of star-forming gas and dust known as the Pillars of Creation, lies outside the field. The pillars became famous through an earlier Hubble image. The nebula lies about 7,000 light-years away.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.23 x 3.36 arcminutes) and distance (7000 light years), the frame spans roughly 6.6 × 6.8 light-years. Its light set out about 7,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys made this image. A near-infrared filter (F775W) is colored red and a blue filter (F475W) is colored blue, with a green channel filled in to complete the color.
understand.eye: Exposures of an hour through one filter and 54 minutes through the other, including near-infrared light the eye cannot see, reveal far more than a visual observer would.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Messier 16 is in Serpens Cauda, the Tail of the Serpent, between Aquila, Sagittarius and Ophiuchus. Amateur telescopes can show it too. A small one picks up broad faint patches of nebula, while a 30 cm instrument or bigger might show the dark pillars on a good night. Hubble's view relies on its 2.4-meter mirror.
alt: Bright young stars embedded in glowing gas in the outer part of the Eagle Nebula.
